ASC_fullwidth_digits_and_space.description: Full-width letter, full-width digits and an ideographic space
ASC_fullwidth_digits_and_space.notes: Derived from the same documented full-width-to-half-width rule: U+FF21 -> A, U+FF11/FF12/FF13 -> 1/2/3, and U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE -> U+0020 half-width space, giving the five-character string "A123 " (trailing half-width space); MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'A123 ', got 'A123\u3000'

ASC_length_preserved.description: The conversion is character-for-character, so the length is unchanged
ASC_length_preserved.notes: Excel documents ASC as changing full-width characters to half-width characters, a one-for-one character mapping rather than an encoding change, so a five-character input yields a five-character result. This case separates a genuine width conversion from a byte-level reinterpretation

ASIN_documented_radians.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arcsine of -0.5 in radians (-pi/6)
ASIN_documented_radians.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -0.523598776. Independently verified in Python: math.asin(-0.5) = -0.5235987755982989, which is exactly -pi/6 -> -0.523598776 at 9 dp

ASIN_documented_degrees.description: The same example converted to degrees, as the documented Remark suggests
ASIN_documented_degrees.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -30. Independently verified: -pi/6 radians = -30 degrees exactly; the double-precision product is -30.000000000000004, which is -30 at 9 dp

ASIN_out_of_domain_num.description: An argument above 1 is outside the documented domain
ASIN_out_of_domain_num.notes: Excel documents that number "must be from -1 to 1"; an argument outside the domain of a real-valued math function is Excel's documented #NUM! case

ASIN_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the ACOT page states it explicitly for this inverse-trigonometric family

ASINH_documented_negative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic sine of -2.5
ASINH_documented_negative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -1.647231146. Independently verified in Python: math.asinh(-2.5) = -1.6472311463710958 = ln(-2.5 + sqrt(7.25)) -> -1.647231146 at 9 dp

ASINH_documented_ten.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic sine of 10
ASINH_documented_ten.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2.99822295. Independently verified in Python: math.asinh(10) = 2.99822295029797 = ln(10 + sqrt(101)) -> 2.99822295 at 8 dp

ASINH_at_zero.description: The inverse hyperbolic sine of zero, which the documented identity ASINH(SINH(x)) = x forces to be zero
ASINH_at_zero.notes: Excel documents "ASINH(SINH(number)) equals number" and sinh(0) = 0, so asinh(0) = 0 exactly. Unlike ACOSH, the documented domain here is "any real number", so zero is inside it

ASINH_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the ACOT page states it explicitly for this inverse-hyperbolic family

ATAN_documented_radians.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of 1 in radians (pi/4)
ATAN_documented_radians.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.785398163. Independently verified in Python: math.atan(1) = 0.7853981633974483, which is exactly pi/4 -> 0.785398163 at 9 dp

ATAN_documented_degrees.description: The same example converted to degrees with the DEGREES function, as the page's third example does
ATAN_documented_degrees.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 45. Independently verified: pi/4 radians = 45 degrees exactly, and the double-precision conversion is exactly 45.0

ATAN_at_zero.notes: tan(0) = 0 and the documented output range is -pi/2 to pi/2, which contains exactly one angle with tangent zero, so ATAN(0) = 0 exactly

ATAN_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the ACOT page states it explicitly for this inverse-trigonometric family

ATAN2_documented_first_quadrant.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (1,1), which is pi/4
ATAN2_documented_first_quadrant.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.785398163. Independently verified in Python: Excel's argument order is ATAN2(x_num, y_num), so this is math.atan2(1, 1) = 0.7853981633974483 = pi/4 -> 0.785398163 at 9 dp

ATAN2_documented_third_quadrant.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: arctangent of the point (-1,-1), which is -3*pi/4
ATAN2_documented_third_quadrant.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -2.35619449. Independently verified: math.atan2(-1, -1) = -2.356194490192345 = -3*pi/4 -> -2.35619449 at 8 dp. This case also pins the documented argument ORDER: a function taking (y, x) instead would still return -3*pi/4 here, but the first-quadrant and x=0 cases below separate the two conventions

ATAN2_documented_degrees.description: The same example converted to degrees with the DEGREES function, as the page's fourth example does
ATAN2_documented_degrees.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -135. Independently verified: -3*pi/4 radians = -135 degrees exactly

ATAN2_zero_x_coordinate.description: An x-coordinate of zero, which the documentation explicitly allows
ATAN2_zero_x_coordinate.notes: Excel documents "ATAN2(a,b) equals ATAN(b/a), except that a can equal 0 in ATAN2". With x_num = 0 and y_num = 1 the point is straight up the y-axis, so the angle from the x-axis is pi/2. Independently verified: math.atan2(1, 0) = 1.5707963267948966 -> 1.570796327 at 9 dp

ATAN2_both_zero_div0.description: Both coordinates zero, which has no defined angle
ATAN2_both_zero_div0.notes: Excel documents: "If both x_num and y_num are 0, ATAN2 returns the #DIV/0! error value." Note this is #DIV/0!, not the #NUM! that most out-of-domain math arguments produce; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#DIV/0!', got 0

ATANH_documented_near_one.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic tangent of 0.76159416
ATANH_documented_near_one.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 1.00000001. ATANH_documented_negative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: inverse hyperbolic tangent of -0.1
ATANH_documented_negative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as -0.100335348. Independently verified in Python: math.atanh(-0.1) = -0.10033534773107558 -> -0.100335348 at 9 dp

ATANH_at_one_num.description: An argument of exactly 1 is excluded by the documented open interval
ATANH_at_one_num.notes: Excel documents "Number must be between -1 and 1 (excluding -1 and 1)"; at 1 the inverse hyperbolic tangent diverges, which is Excel's documented #NUM! case; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

ATANH_text_argument_value.notes: #VALUE! is Excel's documented error for an argument of the wrong type; the ACOT page states it explicitly for this inverse-hyperbolic family

BESSELI_documented_1_5_order_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: modified Bessel function I at x=1.5, order 1
BESSELI_documented_1_5_order_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.981666428. Independently re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besseli(1, 1.5) = 0.98166642857790758565, so the true value rounds to 0.981666429 at 9 dp -- the page's trailing 8 is a TRUNCATION of ...4285 rather than a round. Asserting at 8 dp (0.98166643) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the true value agree, so a mismatch here is an engine difference and not a documentation artefact

BESSELI_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELI_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 1.9 must behave exactly as order 1 and return the same 0.98166643 as the documented example above. Independently verified with mpmath: besseli(1, 1.5) = 0.9816664285779076; besseli(1.9, 1.5) would be 0.38286062, so this case distinguishes truncation from a real fractional-order evaluation

BESSELI_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELI returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELJ_documented_1_9_order_2.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: Bessel function J at x=1.9, order 2
BESSELJ_documented_1_9_order_2.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.329925829, but that figure is WRONG in the 7th decimal place. Re-derived to 20 significant digits with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.32992572769238721660 (scipy.special.jv agrees to machine precision), which differs from the published 0.329925829 by 1.01e-07 -- far larger than the ~1e-10 rounding residue seen on the sibling BESSELY page. Asserting at 6 dp (0.329926) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the mathematically correct value still agree, so this case tests the function rather than Microsoft's typo

BESSELJ_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero
BESSELJ_order_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If n is not an integer, it is truncated", so order 2.7 must behave exactly as order 2. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(2, 1.9) = 0.3299257276923872, while a genuine fractional-order besselj(2.7, 1.9) would be about 0.16248, so this case separates truncation from fractional-order evaluation

BESSELJ_zero_order_at_zero.description: The order-0 Bessel function at the origin
BESSELJ_zero_order_at_zero.notes: Follows from the documented series definition on the page: J_0(0) is the k=0 term (-1)^0/(0! * Gamma(1)) * (0/2)^0 = 1, with every later term carrying a positive power of x/2 and vanishing. Independently verified with mpmath: besselj(0, 0) = 1.0 exactly

BESSELJ_negative_order_num.notes: Excel documents: "If n < 0, BESSELJ returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BESSELJ_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELJ returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELK_documented_1_5_order_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: modified Bessel function K at x=1.5, order 1
BESSELK_documented_1_5_order_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.277387804. BESSELK_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero

BESSELK_text_x_value.notes: Excel documents: "If x is nonnumeric, BESSELK returns the #VALUE! error value."

BESSELY_order_truncated.description: A non-integer order, which the documentation says is truncated toward zero

BETA.DIST_doc_cumulative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: cumulative beta distribution at x=2 with alpha=8, beta=10 on the interval [1,3]
BETA.DIST_doc_cumulative.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.6854706. Independently derived from the documented definition (the beta CDF rescaled to [A,B]): I_{(x-A)/(B-A)}(alpha,beta) = I_{0.5}(8,10), the regularized incomplete beta function, which scipy.special.betainc(8,10,0.5) gives as 0.6854705810546875 -> 0.6854706 at 7 dp

BETA.DIST_doc_density.description: The same parameters with cumulative FALSE, returning the probability density
BETA.DIST_doc_density.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 1.4837646. Independently derived from the beta density rescaled to [A,B]: f((x-A)/(B-A); 8,10)/(B-A) = beta.pdf(0.5,8,10)/2 = 2.967529296875/2 = 1.4837646484374996 -> 1.4837646 at 7 dp

BETA.DIST_standard_interval.description: The same distribution on the default interval, with A and B omitted
BETA.DIST_standard_interval.notes: Excel documents "If you omit values for A and B, BETA.DIST uses the standard cumulative beta distribution, so that A = 0 and B = 1". Because x=2 on [1,3] rescales to exactly 0.5 on [0,1], this must return the identical 0.6854706 as the documented example -- a direct check of the documented default-bounds rule

BETA.DIST_alpha_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETA.DIST returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BETA.DIST_x_above_upper_num.description: An x value above the upper bound B
BETA.DIST_x_above_upper_num.notes: Excel documents: "If x < A, x > B, or A = B, BETA.DIST returns the #NUM! error value." Here x = 4 exceeds B = 3; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BETA.DIST_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETA.DIST returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETA.INV_doc_roundtrip.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the inverse of the cumulative beta distribution at probability 0.685470581, alpha=8, beta=10 on [1,3]
BETA.INV_doc_roundtrip.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 2. Independently derived from the documented inverse relationship ("BETA.INV seeks that value x such that BETA.DIST(x, alpha, beta, TRUE, A, B) = probability"): A + (B-A)*betaincinv(8,10,0.685470581) = 1 + 2*0.4999999999815714 = 1.9999999999631428 -> 2 at 6 dp. The tiny shortfall comes from the input probability itself being the 9-dp rounding of BETA.DIST(2,8,10,TRUE,1,3), so 6 dp is the honest assertion depth

BETA.INV_standard_median.description: The median of a Beta(2,3) distribution on the default [0,1] interval
BETA.INV_standard_median.notes: Excel documents that omitting A and B uses the standard beta distribution on [0,1]. Independently derived: scipy.special.betaincinv(2,3,0.5) = 0.3857275681323895 -> 0.3857276 at 7 dp

BETA.INV_probability_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If probability <= 0 or probability > 1, BETA.INV returns the #NUM! error value." Note the asymmetry -- probability = 1 is allowed but probability = 0 is not; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got 1

BETA.INV_probability_above_one_num.notes: Excel documents the same rule for probability > 1; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BETA.INV_beta_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETA.INV returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BETA.INV_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, BETA.INV returns the #VALUE! error value."

BETADIST_doc_cumulative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example for the legacy (pre-2010) name: cumulative beta distribution at x=2, alpha=8, beta=10 on [1,3]

BETADIST_standard_interval.description: The same distribution on the default interval, with A and B omitted

BETADIST_beta_zero_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or beta <= 0, BETADIST returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

BETADIST_x_below_lower_num.description: An x value below the lower bound A

BETAINV_standard_median.description: The median of a Beta(8,10) distribution on the default [0,1] interval

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_single.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: probability of exactly 48 successes in 60 trials at p=0.75

BINOM.DIST.RANGE_doc_range.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.524 (52.4%). BINOM.DIST.RANGE_single_6dp.description: The same single-value example asserted at full precision rather than the page's 3 dp

BINOM.DIST_doc_pmf.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.2050781. Independently derived from the documented probability mass function COMBIN(n,x)*p^x*(1-p)^(n-x): C(10,6)*0.5^10 = 210/1024 = 0.205078125 exactly -> 0.2050781 at 7 dp

BINOM.INV_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 4. CELL_type_value.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "v" for a cell holding a value
CELL_type_value.notes: Excel documents info_type "type" as returning "'v' for value if the cell contains anything else" (that is, anything other than blank or a text constant). A1 holds the number 42

CELL_type_label.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "l" for a cell holding a text constant
CELL_type_label.notes: Excel documents "type" as returning "'l' for label if the cell contains a text constant". A2 holds the text "hello"

CELL_type_blank.description: The documented "type" info_type returns "b" for an empty cell
CELL_type_blank.notes: Excel documents "type" as returning "'b' for blank if the cell is empty". A3 is deliberately left unset. EXCLUSIONS: this corpus tests only the four deterministic info_types "row", "col", "contents" and "type". The others are deliberately omitted because their results are not a property of the formula: "address" and "filename" depend on the workbook's path and quoting (and "filename" is documented to return empty text for an unsaved sheet); "format", "color", "parentheses", "prefix", "protect" and "width" depend on cell formatting, column width and sheet protection that survive an .xlsx round-trip inconsistently, and Microsoft documents all six as unsupported in Excel for the web, Excel Mobile and Excel Starter; and the reference-omitted form CELL(info_type) is excluded because Microsoft's own page warns it reports "your active cell" at calculation time and "does not reliably produce information about a specific cell" -- it is volatile by design and could not be asserted against any fixed value

CHISQ.TEST_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.0003082 and states the underlying statistic is 16.16957 with 2 degrees of freedom. CONFIDENCE.NORM_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 95% confidence half-width for a population standard deviation of 2.5 and a sample of 50
CONFIDENCE.NORM_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's CONFIDENCE.NORM page publishes this example's result rounded to 0.692952; its CONFIDENCE page publishes the identical calculation to more digits as 0.692951912, and the two agree. Independently derived from the documented normal-distribution half-width z_(1-alpha/2) * standard_dev / sqrt(size): scipy.stats.norm.isf(0.05/2) = 1.9599639845400545, so 1.9599639845400545 * 2.5 / sqrt(50) = 0.6929519121748391 -> 0.692951912 at 9 dp. Asserted at 9 dp rather than the page's 6 because the deeper figure is derived, not merely copied

CONFIDENCE.NORM_size_truncated.description: A non-integer sample size, which the documentation says is truncated
CONFIDENCE.NORM_size_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If size is not an integer, it is truncated", so 50.9 must behave exactly as 50. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine size of 50.9 would give 1.9599639845400545 * 2.5 / sqrt(50.9) = 0.686798

CONFIDENCE.NORM_alpha_one_num.notes: Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or alpha >= 1, CONFIDENCE.NORM returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

CONFIDENCE.NORM_negative_standard_dev_nu.notes: Excel documents: "If standard_dev <= 0, CONFIDENCE.NORM returns the #NUM! error value."; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

CONFIDENCE.T_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 95% Student-t confidence half-width for a standard deviation of 1 and a sample of 50
CONFIDENCE.T_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.284196855. Independently derived from the documented Student-t half-width t_(1-alpha/2, size-1) * standard_dev / sqrt(size): scipy.stats.t.isf(0.05/2, 49) = 2.0095752371292397 on size-1 = 49 degrees of freedom, so 2.0095752371292397 * 1 / sqrt(50) = 0.2841968554957299 -> 0.284196855 at 9 dp. The t multiplier is visibly larger than the normal 1.95996 of CONFIDENCE.NORM, which is what distinguishes the two functions

CONFIDENCE.T_size_truncated.description: A non-integer sample size, which the documentation says is truncated
CONFIDENCE.T_size_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If size is not an integer, it is truncated", so 50.9 must behave exactly as 50. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine size of 50.9 (49.9 degrees of freedom) would give 0.281545

CONFIDENCE.T_size_one_div0.notes: Excel documents: "If size equals 1, CONFIDENCE.T returns #DIV/0! error value." This is the one place the .T variant's error contract differs from CONFIDENCE.NORM's, which returns #NUM! only below size 1 and computes normally at size 1: with size 1 there are zero degrees of freedom for the t distribution

COPILOT_exists_probe.description: Existence probe only: COPILOT sends a prompt to an Azure-hosted AI model, so its output is neither deterministic nor reproducible; this case only records whether the engine recognizes the function name at all
COPILOT_exists_probe.notes: NOT ASSERTABLE BY DESIGN, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. Microsoft's page states the function "calls an AI model hosted on Azure directly from a cell formula", requires an active internet connection and a qualifying Copilot licence, currently uses gpt-4.1-mini (2025-04-14), and that "formula results may change over time, even with the same arguments" -- so there is no value any engine could be held to. The page also announces that from 2026-09-14 the COPILOT function will no longer be available in Excel at all. Without a licence Excel itself documents #BLOCKED ("License Not Found"), so a non-Excel engine returning #NAME? tells us the name is unknown, which is the only comparable datum here

COS_doc_radians.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cosine of 1.047 radians
COS_doc_radians.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5001711. Independently derived: math.cos(1.047) = 0.5001710745970701 -> 0.5001711 at 7 dp. 1.047 is a decimal approximation of pi/3, which is why the result sits just above 0.5

COS_doc_degrees_via_pi.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 60 degrees converted to radians by multiplying by PI()/180
COS_doc_degrees_via_pi.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5, and cos(60 degrees) = cos(pi/3) = 1/2 exactly. In IEEE double arithmetic math.cos(math.pi/3) evaluates to 0.5000000000000001, one unit in the last place above 0.5, so the assertion is made at 9 dp where the exact and floating-point values agree

COS_doc_degrees_via_radians_fn.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the same 60 degrees converted with the RADIANS function instead
COS_doc_degrees_via_radians_fn.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5 as well. Exactly the same mathematics as the previous case; the point of running both is that Excel documents RADIANS and the explicit PI()/180 multiplication as interchangeable, so a divergence between the two rows would be an engine quirk in RADIANS rather than in COS

COS_at_zero.notes: Follows from the definition of the cosine, cos(0) = 1 exactly, with no rounding needed: this anchors the function at a point where any floating-point implementation must be exact

COSH_doc_4.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cosine of 4
COSH_doc_4.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 27.308233. Independently derived from the documented formula cosh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/2: math.cosh(4) = 27.308232836016487, and (math.exp(4)+math.exp(-4))/2 gives the same to machine precision -> 27.308233 at 6 dp

COSH_doc_exp_1.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cosine of e, the base of the natural logarithm
COSH_doc_exp_1.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 7.6101251. Independently derived: math.cosh(math.e) = 7.610125138662288 -> 7.6101251 at 7 dp

COSH_at_zero.notes: From the documented formula (e^0 + e^0)/2 = (1+1)/2 = 1 exactly. cosh is bounded below by 1, so this is also its minimum

COSH_is_even.description: The hyperbolic cosine of -4, which must equal that of +4
COSH_is_even.notes: cosh is an even function: the documented formula (e^x + e^-x)/2 is unchanged when x is replaced by -x, so COSH(-4) must return exactly the documented COSH(4) value of 27.308233. Verified independently: math.cosh(-4) = 27.308232836016487, bit-identical to math.cosh(4)

COT_doc_30.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cotangent of 30 radians
COT_doc_30.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as -0.156. Independently derived from the documented identity COT(n) = 1/TAN(n): 1/math.tan(30) = -0.15611995216165922 -> -0.156119952 at 9 dp, which agrees with the published -0.156 at the depth the page prints. Asserted at 9 dp because the deeper figure is derived rather than copied. Note the argument is 30 RADIANS, not 30 degrees, which is why the value is negative

COT_doc_cell_reference_45.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cotangent of the value 45 held in a cell
COT_doc_cell_reference_45.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as 0.617. Independently derived: 1/math.tan(45) = 0.6173696237835551 -> 0.617369624 at 9 dp, which agrees with the published 0.617

COT_zero_div0.notes: Excel documents: "COT(0) returns the #DIV/0! error value." This follows from the documented identity COT(n) = 1/TAN(n) with TAN(0) = 0, and is a different error class from the #NUM! the same page specifies for out-of-range arguments. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return #NUM! here, i.e. they collapse the two documented error classes onto the out-of-range one; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#DIV/0!', got '#NUM!'

COT_out_of_range_num.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27
COT_out_of_range_num.notes: Excel documents: "The absolute value of Number must be less than 2^27" and "If Number is outside its constraints, COT returns the #NUM! error value." 2^27 = 134217728 is exactly the excluded boundary. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds ignore this range check and return -0.846108835418734 instead of the documented error -- and that number is not garbage: cot(2^27) re-derived with mpmath at 60 digits is -0.84610883541873383485, so LibreOffice's argument reduction is accurate to full double precision here and it simply declines to refuse an input Excel refuses; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got -0.846108835418734

COT_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If Number is a non-numeric value, COT returns the #VALUE! error value."

COTH_doc_2.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cotangent of 2
COTH_doc_2.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as 1.037. Independently derived from the documented relationship coth(x) = 1/tanh(x) = (e^x + e^-x)/(e^x - e^-x): 1/math.tanh(2) = 1.0373147207275482 -> 1.037314721 at 9 dp, agreeing with the published 1.037 at the depth the page prints

COTH_is_odd.description: The hyperbolic cotangent of -2, which must be the negative of that of +2
COTH_is_odd.notes: coth is an odd function: (e^-x + e^x)/(e^-x - e^x) is the negative of (e^x + e^-x)/(e^x - e^-x), so COTH(-2) must be exactly -COTH(2). Verified independently: 1/math.tanh(-2) = -1.0373147207275482

COTH_out_of_range_num.description: An argument at the documented magnitude limit of 2^27
COTH_out_of_range_num.notes: Excel documents: "The absolute value of Number must be less than 2^27" and "If Number is outside its constraints, COTH returns the #NUM! error value." 2^27 = 134217728 is exactly the excluded boundary. Mathematically coth(134217728) is indistinguishable from 1, so this case tests the documented range check rather than the arithmetic. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return 1 instead of the documented error, i.e. they answer the mathematics and ignore the range check; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got 1

COTH_text_argument_value.notes: Excel documents: "If Number is a non-numeric value, COTH returns the #VALUE! error value."

COUPDAYBS_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: days from the start of the coupon period to settlement, semiannual, actual/actual
COUPDAYBS_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 71. Setup serials are the dates Microsoft's page prints: 40568 = 2011-01-25 (settlement), 40862 = 2011-11-15 (maturity), frequency 2 (semiannual), basis 1 (actual/actual). Counting coupon dates back from maturity in six-month steps gives 2011-11-15, 2011-05-15, 2010-11-15, so the settlement date falls in the coupon period 2010-11-15 to 2011-05-15. On basis 1 the count is the actual number of days from 2010-11-15 to 2011-01-25: 15 remaining days in November + 31 in December + 25 in January = 71, confirmed by Python date subtraction

COUPDAYBS_basis_0_30_360.notes: Basis 0 is documented as US (NASD) 30/360, which counts every month as 30 days: from 2010-11-15 to 2011-01-25 that is (2011-2010)*360 + (1-11)*30 + (25-15) = 360 - 300 + 10 = 70, one day fewer than the actual/actual 71. This case discriminates the basis argument, which the documented example alone does not

CRITBINOM_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: smallest k whose cumulative binomial probability over 6 fair trials reaches 0.75
CRITBINOM_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 4. Independently derived by summing the binomial probabilities explicitly: with trials 6 and probability 0.5 the cumulative sums are 0.015625, 0.109375, 0.34375, 0.65625, 0.890625, 0.984375, 1.0 for k = 0..6. The first sum that is >= the criterion 0.75 is 0.890625 at k = 4, which is the documented answer

CRITBINOM_higher_alpha.description: The same trials and probability at a stricter criterion of 0.9
CRITBINOM_higher_alpha.notes: From the same explicit cumulative sums, the first value >= 0.9 is 0.984375 at k = 5 (the cumulative sum at k = 4 is 0.890625, just short). This case discriminates the alpha argument and pins the >= comparison direction

CRITBINOM_trials_truncated.description: A non-integer number of trials, which the documentation says is truncated
CRITBINOM_trials_truncated.notes: Excel documents "If trials is not an integer, it is truncated", so 6.9 must behave exactly as 6. With 6 trials the cumulative sums are 0.015625, 0.109375, 0.34375, 0.65625, ...; the first one >= the criterion 0.6 is 0.65625 at k = 3. The criterion 0.6 was chosen precisely because it discriminates: with 7 trials the sums are 0.0078125, 0.0625, 0.2265625, 0.5, 0.7734375, ... and the first >= 0.6 is at k = 4, so an engine that rounded 6.9 up to 7 instead of truncating would return 4 here. (At the page's own criterion of 0.75 both 6 and 7 trials give 4, which is why this case does not reuse it)

CSC_doc_15.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result to three decimals as 1.538. CUBEKPIMEMBER_no_cube_connection_probe.description: Existence probe only: the KPI-member form from Microsoft's own example, against a connection name that does not exist in this workbook. No OLAP connection can exist in a flat workbook, so this records what the engine actually returns rather than asserting a documented value
CUBEKPIMEMBER_no_cube_connection_probe.notes: NOT EXECUTABLE AS DOCUMENTED, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. Microsoft documents this function as returning data from an OLAP cube reached through a named workbook connection -- the CUBEKPIMEMBER page states outright that the cube functions are "supported only when the workbook is connected to a Microsoft SQL Server 2005 Analysis Services or later data source". A flat .xlsx carries no such connection, and neither LibreOffice Calc nor Google Sheets can supply one, so the documented behaviour cannot be reproduced by this harness in any engine. Microsoft's page documents that "if the connection name is not a valid workbook connection stored in the workbook, CUBEKPIMEMBER returns a #NAME? error value", and the same for an OLAP server that is not running. The trap this case exists to avoid: Excel itself documents that an invalid connection name yields #NAME?, which is the SAME token an engine emits for a function it has never heard of. A #NAME? here therefore does NOT distinguish "present but unconnected" from "absent", and this case is recorded with no asserted expected value so it can never be scored as documented behaviour. What the run does establish is recorded separately: probing all four pinned LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) with the plain name, the _xlfn. storage form and the COM.MICROSOFT. add-in form returned #NAME? for all three spellings on every build, which is the signature of a name the engine does not implement at all rather than of a missing data connection

DBCS_halfwidth_latin_to_fullwidth.description: Half-width (single-byte) Latin letters converted to full-width
DBCS_halfwidth_latin_to_fullwidth.notes: Microsoft's DBCS page documents the rule as: "converts half-width (single-byte) letters within a character string to full-width (double-byte) characters", and adds "If text does not contain any half-width English letters or katakana, text is not changed". The page also warns that "The name of the function (and the characters that it converts) depends upon your language settings"; this harness runs under LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8, a non-DBCS default language, which is stated here rather than assumed away. PUBLISHED EXAMPLE CONTRADICTS THE PUBLISHED RULE: the page's first worked example reads '=DBCS("EXCEL") equals "EXCEL"', i.e. it shows the argument coming back unchanged -- which is the documented behaviour of the INVERSE function ASC, whose page carries the identical line, and is impossible under DBCS's own stated rule because "EXCEL" is five half-width English letters. The value asserted here is derived from the rule instead: E X C E L map to U+FF25 U+FF38 U+FF23 U+FF25 U+FF2C (FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL E X C E L), exactly the inverse of the mapping batch A's ASC cases assert in the other direction. The page's second example, which does show a conversion, is rendered as inline GIF images (media/fe337.gif ...) so no literal argument can be copied from it. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) return #NAME? -- and a name-form probe confirms this is a genuine gap rather than a storage-prefix artefact: the plain name, the _xlfn. storage form and the COM.MICROSOFT. add-in form all return #NAME? on every build. LibreOffice nevertheless PERFORMS this conversion under a different name: on all four builds '=JIS("EXCEL")' returns exactly the full-width string asserted here, which independently confirms both the derived expected value and that the gap is a missing alias, not a missing capability.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'ＥＸＣＥＬ', got '#NAME?'

DBCS_fullwidth_unchanged.description: Text that is already full-width is returned unchanged
DBCS_fullwidth_unchanged.notes: Microsoft's DBCS page documents the rule as: "converts half-width (single-byte) letters within a character string to full-width (double-byte) characters", and adds "If text does not contain any half-width English letters or katakana, text is not changed". The page also warns that "The name of the function (and the characters that it converts) depends upon your language settings"; this harness runs under LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8, a non-DBCS default language, which is stated here rather than assumed away. This case is unambiguous under either reading of the page: the argument contains no half-width English letters or katakana, so the documented no-change clause applies and the result is the argument itself. EXECUTED RESULT: #NAME? on all four LibreOffice builds; see DBCS_halfwidth_latin_to_fullwidth for the three-spelling probe and for LibreOffice's JIS equivalent.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'ＥＸＣＥＬ', got '#NAME?'

DBCS_roundtrip_through_ASC.description: Round trip: converting to full-width and back to half-width
DBCS_roundtrip_through_ASC.notes: Deliberately locale-independent, and the reason this case exists. If DBCS converts (the documented rule), ASC converts back and the result is "EXCEL"; if DBCS is a no-op under a non-DBCS default language, ASC leaves the already-half-width text alone and the result is still "EXCEL". Both readings of Microsoft's page agree here, so a failure of this case cannot be blamed on the harness locale -- it can only mean the engine lacks one of the two functions or mangles the text. EXECUTED RESULT: #NAME? on all four LibreOffice builds. Because ASC itself is supported there (batch A executed it), the failure is entirely DBCS's, which is what this locale-independent case was built to establish.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 'EXCEL', got '#NAME?'

DBCS_length_preserved.description: The conversion is character-for-character, so the length is unchanged
DBCS_length_preserved.notes: Microsoft documents DBCS as changing half-width characters to full-width characters -- a one-for-one character mapping, not an encoding change -- so a five-character input yields a five-character result whether or not the mapping fires. This is the mirror of batch A's ASC_length_preserved case and separates a genuine width conversion from a byte-level reinterpretation. EXECUTED RESULT: #NAME? on all four LibreOffice builds -- LEN is supported, so the unrecognized name is DBCS.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 5, got '#NAME?'

DCOUNTA_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: non-blank Profit cells among the apple trees between 10 and 16 feet tall
DCOUNTA_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes this example as '=DCOUNTA(A6:E12, "Profit", A3:F4)' with the result 1 and the explanation "Counts the rows (1) containing 'Apple' in column A with a height >10 and <16. Only row 8 satisfies these three conditions." Criteria A3:F4 is the header row plus the single condition row (Apple, Height >10, Height <16), which selects only the Apple/14ft record; its Profit cell is non-blank, so the count is 1. Set up from Microsoft's own worked example for the database functions: the orchard table, which is one criteria header row, two criteria rows, a database header row and six records. HARNESS PLACEMENT: the page pastes the table at A1, but this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1, which the table's second "Height" criteria header would occupy, so the whole block is pasted two rows lower instead. Every relative offset the page describes is preserved -- the database header is still the row immediately below the last criteria row -- which puts the criteria at A3:F5 and the database at A6:E12 here. One further deviation: the page writes its tree criteria as the cell entry ="=Apple" (the documented trick for storing the literal text =Apple, which forces an exact match). openpyxl cannot author that cell -- any string beginning with = is serialized as a formula -- so the criteria cells here hold the plain text Apple and Pear. On this data the two forms select the same records, because no other tree name in the table begins with "Apple" or "Pear".

DISC_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the discount rate of a bond priced at 97.975 per 100 face value, actual/actual basis
DISC_doc_example.notes: MICROSOFT-PUBLISHED RESULT CORRECTED. The page's example data is settlement 07/01/2018, maturity 01/01/2048, price 97.975, redemption 100, basis 1 (actual/actual), and it publishes the result 0.001038. That figure does not belong to those inputs. Derived independently from the formula the page itself states, DISC = ((redemption - pr)/redemption) * (B/DSM): (100 - 97.975)/100 = 0.02025, DSM = 10776 actual days from 2018-07-01 to 2048-01-01, and B under the documented actual/actual basis is the average length of the calendar years spanned, giving a year fraction of 29.50242868497748 and a discount rate of 0.0006863841691213483. The published 0.001038 is reproducible only by moving the maturity back ten years: with maturity 01/01/2038 the same arithmetic gives 0.0010381908237747707, which rounds to exactly the printed 0.001038. The published number is therefore a stale figure left behind when the example's dates were rolled forward, not a rounding of the correct answer, so the correct value is asserted here and the discrepancy recorded rather than buried. Asserted at 12 decimal places (0.000686384169), which is roughly 9 significant digits of the independently derived value and well inside double precision; the ROUND() wrapper keeps the assertion free of last-bit formatting differences. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return 0.000686384169121348, matching the independently derived value to full double precision -- so LibreOffice agrees with the derivation and with the page's stated inputs, and it is Microsoft's printed 0.001038 that stands alone.

DISC_price_zero_num.description: A price of zero, which the documentation excludes

DURATION_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: a 30-year 8% bond yielding 9%, semiannual, actual/actual basis
DURATION_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 10.9191453. Derived independently from the documented definition, "the Macauley duration for an assumed par value of $100 ... the weighted average of the present value of cash flows". Settlement 2018-07-01 falls exactly on a coupon date of the 2048-01-01 maturity at semiannual frequency, so there are 59 remaining coupons at times 0.5, 1.0, ... 29.5 years; discounting each 4.00 coupon (plus 100 redemption at t = 29.5) at 9% nominal semiannual and taking the cash-flow-weighted mean time gives 10.919145281591925, which rounds to the published 10.9191453 at 7 dp. EXECUTED RESULT -- SILENT WRONG VALUE, the most serious class in this batch. All four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) return 10.9215739665694 where both Microsoft's published figure and the independent derivation give 10.919145281591925: a plausible number, no error, wrong in the third decimal (2.2e-4 relative). The mechanism is pinned down exactly rather than guessed. The discrepancy is 10.9215739665694 - 10.9191452815919 = 0.0024286849775, and YEARFRAC over the same two dates on the same basis 1 returns 29.5024286849775 where the coupon schedule gives 59 coupons / 2 per year = 29.5 exactly -- the excess, 0.0024286849775, matches the error to twelve digits. LibreOffice is therefore taking the cash-flow times from an actual/actual year fraction instead of from the coupon count, which shifts EVERY cash flow later by the same amount and so shifts the weighted average by that amount. The companion case DURATION_basis_30_360 is the control: on basis 0, where YEARFRAC over these dates is exactly 29.5, all four builds return 10.9191452815919 and agree with the documented value.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 10.9191453, got 10.921574

DURATION_basis_30_360.description: The same bond on the US 30/360 basis instead of actual/actual
DURATION_basis_30_360.notes: Derived, not published: this case exists as a controlled comparison against DURATION_doc_example. Because settlement lands exactly on a coupon date, the cash-flow schedule is identical under every basis, so the Macaulay duration is the same 10.919145281591925 whichever basis is chosen -- and the two cases together therefore isolate whether an engine's basis handling leaks into the duration. Note that YEARFRAC over the same two dates is exactly 29.5 on basis 0 but 29.50242868497748 on basis 1, which is the quantity that separates the two cases on an engine that derives the schedule from a year fraction. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds return 10.9191452815919, matching the derivation exactly -- while the otherwise identical actual/actual case (DURATION_doc_example) does not. The pair isolates the defect to LibreOffice's basis-1 year fraction; see that case's note for the arithmetic.

FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT_value_probe.description: Existence and value probe: the 95% confidence radius one step past the end of a seasonal series, recorded WITHOUT an asserted expected value
FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT_value_probe.notes: NO NUMERIC VALUE IS ASSERTED, deliberately, and for two independent reasons. FIRST, Microsoft's FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT page publishes no worked example at all -- it offers only a "Download a sample workbook" link -- and the underlying AAA (additive-error/additive-trend/additive-season) exponential-smoothing algorithm is specified in the documentation by behaviour, not by a reproducible formula: the smoothing parameters are fitted by an optimizer whose starting values, convergence tolerance and interval-estimation method are all implementation freedom. Nothing on the page lets an outside party derive a figure, and this corpus does not assert figures it cannot derive. SECOND, and decisively: LIBREOFFICE'S FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT IS NOT DETERMINISTIC, which is established here rather than inferred. Five byte-identical =FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(21,C1:C20,A1:A20) formulas placed in five cells of ONE workbook return five DIFFERENT values in a single recalculation (e.g. on 25.8.7.3: 2.60005581814345, 2.62116197822427, 2.62767831058431, 2.56740494916855, 2.63866315142705), and the same file converted three times running gives three more different sets. The spread is roughly +/-4% and it is not build-specific -- every one of all four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) behaves this way. FORECAST.ETS.STAT's RMSE on the identical data, by contrast, is 1.63757980666069 on every cell, every run and every build, so the non-determinism is confined to the interval estimate and is not general flakiness in the harness or the engine. Excel's CONFINT is a deterministic function of its inputs. This is why no numeric value is asserted for CONFINT anywhere in this corpus: an asserted figure would be a coin flip, and recording one would be worse than recording none. HARNESS DATA (identical on every FORECAST.ETS.* case in this batch, and deliberately synthetic so the seasonal structure is a fact about the data rather than a guess): A1:A20 is the timeline 1..20, a constant step of 1. B1:B20 is a textbook-clean series of period 4 -- 10, 20, 30, 20 repeated five times -- so the only repetitive pattern present has length 4. C1:C20 is that same period-4 pattern plus a fixed, hard-coded residual sequence (0, 1, -1, 2, 0, -2, 1, 0, ... ), giving a series with real forecast error but an unambiguous season; nothing here is random, so the input is byte-identical on every run and every build. D1:D20 is the timeline 2, 4, ... 40, a constant step of 2. E1:E20 is the 1..20 timeline with its first two entries both set to 1, i.e. a DUPLICATE timeline value. G1:G20 is strictly linear (7, 9, ... 45) with no seasonal component. H1:H20 is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 33, ... -- a timeline with no constant step at all. Column F is left empty throughout because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT_nonnegative.description: Structural assertion: a confidence RADIUS cannot be negative
FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT_nonnegative.notes: Asserted structurally rather than numerically. Microsoft defines the return value as a radius -- "95% of future points are expected to fall within this radius from the result FORECAST.ETS forecasted" -- and a radius is by definition non-negative. FTEST_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the two-tailed F-test on the two samples
FTEST_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=FTEST(A2:A6,B2:B6)' with the result 0.64831785. Derived independently in Python at 50 digits, and along a different path from any statistics library's F routines: the two sample variances are computed by hand from the data (sample 1 mean 11.6, sum of squared deviations 159.2, variance 159.2/4 = 39.8; sample 2 mean 31.4, sum of squared deviations 259.2, variance 259.2/4 = 64.8), giving the ratio F = 39.8/64.8 = 0.6141975308641975 on 4 and 4 degrees of freedom. The upper-tail probability is then taken from the REGULARIZED INCOMPLETE BETA function rather than from an F distribution routine -- P(F > f) = I_{d2/(d2+d1*f)}(d2/2, d1/2) = 0.67584107660691275 -- and the two-tailed answer is 2*min(p, 1-p) = 0.64831784678617450366, which rounds to exactly the published 0.64831785. This is the same example data, and the same derived value, that batch C asserted for the modern replacement F.TEST; asserting both is the point, because it checks that an engine's legacy alias really is the same function. Derived independently as the REGULARIZED LOWER INCOMPLETE GAMMA function P(alpha, x/beta) = P(9, 5.000005655) = 0.068094003869787331102 at 50 digits, which rounds to exactly the published 0.068094. Asserted at 12 dp: the 11th and 12th decimals (…3870) are carried because they are inside double precision and pin the implementation's incomplete-gamma routine, not just its leading digits. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 10.00001131 (the value at which the distribution is evaluated), A3 = 9 (alpha) and A4 = 2 (beta), pasted at A1 exactly as the page describes. Column F is untouched because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

GAMMA.DIST_alpha_one_is_exponential.description: The page's own identity: at alpha = 1 the gamma distribution IS the exponential distribution
GAMMA.DIST_alpha_one_is_exponential.notes: Microsoft's GAMMA.DIST page states "When alpha = 1, GAMMA.DIST returns the exponential distribution with:" followed by an equation rendered as an image. The identity behind it is standard and independently checkable: the gamma CDF with alpha = 1 and scale beta is 1 - e^(-x/beta). At x = 2, beta = 3 that is 1 - e^(-2/3) = 0.48658288096740797313 (mpmath, 50 digits), and the regularized incomplete gamma P(1, 2/3) gives the identical value. Asserted as a difference of zero against the engine's OWN EXP, so it tests the distribution rather than a printed constant, and so it holds even if the engine's exp differs in the last bit. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 10.00001131 (the value at which the distribution is evaluated), A3 = 9 (alpha) and A4 = 2 (beta), pasted at A1 exactly as the page describes. Column F is untouched because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

GAMMA.DIST_chisq_identity.description: The page's other stated identity, relating the gamma and chi-squared distributions
GAMMA.DIST_chisq_identity.notes: Microsoft's GAMMA.DIST page states: "For a positive integer n, when alpha = n/2, beta = 2, and cumulative = TRUE, GAMMA.DIST returns (1 - CHISQ.DIST.RT(x)) with n degrees of freedom." Instantiated here at n = 4, so alpha = 2 and beta = 2. Derived independently: P(2, 1.5) = 0.44217459962892543 at 50 digits, and the chi-squared survival function at x = 3 with 4 degrees of freedom is 0.55782540037107457, whose complement is the same number. Written as a difference of exactly zero so it tests the two functions against each other inside the engine under test rather than against a figure from outside it. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 10.00001131 (the value at which the distribution is evaluated), A3 = 9 (alpha) and A4 = 2 (beta), pasted at A1 exactly as the page describes. GAMMA.INV_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the inverse of the gamma cumulative distribution
GAMMA.INV_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=GAMMA.INV(A2,A3,A4)' with the result 10.0000112. Derived independently, and deliberately NOT by calling an inverse-gamma routine: the regularized lower incomplete gamma P(9, x/2) was built at 50 digits with mpmath and the equation P(9, x/2) = 0.068094 solved for x by mpmath's own root finder, giving x = 10.000011191437178309. That rounds to exactly the published 10.0000112 at 7 dp, which is the precision the page prints, so 7 is the precision asserted. Note this is NOT the 10.00001131 that appears as the input on the GAMMA.DIST page: the two pages form a round trip, but Microsoft rounded the probability to six decimals (0.068094) before feeding it back, and inverting a rounded probability necessarily lands slightly off the original x. The corpus asserts the value that the published INPUT actually produces, and tests the exact round trip separately below. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 0.068094 (the probability), A3 = 9 (alpha) and A4 = 2 (beta), pasted at A1 as the page describes. Column F is untouched because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

GAMMA.INV_round_trips_with_GAMMA_DIST.description: The documented inverse relationship, without a rounded probability in the middle
GAMMA.INV_round_trips_with_GAMMA_DIST.notes: Excel documents the pair as exact inverses: "If p = GAMMA.DIST(x,...), then GAMMA.INV(p,...) = x." Feeding the FULL-PRECISION cumulative probability back in (rather than Microsoft's 6-decimal 0.068094) must therefore return the original 10.00001131. Derived independently with mpmath: solving P(9, x/2) = 0.068094003869787331102 gives x = 10.00001131 to twenty digits. Asserted at 6 dp because Microsoft's own page warns the inverse is iterative -- "precision of GAMMA.INV depends on precision of GAMMA.DIST" and "GAMMA.INV uses an iterative search technique" -- so the last couple of digits are an implementation's convergence tolerance, not a fact about the function. This case is the one that actually tests the inverse property; the doc-example case above tests the published figure. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 0.068094 (the probability), A3 = 9 (alpha) and A4 = 2 (beta), pasted at A1 as the page describes. Column F is untouched because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

The gamma distribution's support starts at 0 and its CDF is 0 there, so the inverse at probability 0 is 0. GAMMA_doc_example_2_5.notes: Microsoft publishes '=GAMMA(2.5)' with the result 1.329 ("Returns the gamma function value of 2.5 (1.329)"). Derived independently with mpmath at 50 decimal digits: Gamma(2.5) = 1.3293403881791370205, which rounds to the published 1.329 at the three decimals the page prints. Asserted at 12 dp rather than 3 because the page's precision is a display choice, not a limit on the answer, and 12 dp is well inside the ~15 significant digits an IEEE double carries. Cross-checked against the closed form the page itself supplies, Gamma(N+1) = N*Gamma(N): Gamma(2.5) = 1.5*Gamma(1.5) = 1.5*0.5*Gamma(0.5) = 0.75*sqrt(pi) = 1.32934038817913702, identical to 17 digits.

GAMMA_doc_example_negative.description: Microsoft's second worked example: a negative non-integer argument
GAMMA_doc_example_negative.notes: Microsoft publishes '=GAMMA(-3.75)' with the result 0.268. Derived independently with mpmath at 50 digits: Gamma(-3.75) = 0.26786612886141660256, which rounds to the published 0.268. This case matters because the gamma function is only defined for negative arguments by analytic continuation -- an implementation that simply integrates the defining integral cannot reach it -- and because the sign is a real test: Gamma is positive on (-4,-3), and an engine using the reflection formula with a sign slip lands on -0.268.

GAMMA_integer_is_factorial.description: At a positive integer n, GAMMA(n) is (n-1)!
GAMMA_integer_is_factorial.notes: Derived from the recurrence the page states, Gamma(N+1) = N*Gamma(N), together with Gamma(1) = 1: Gamma(5) = 4*3*2*1 = 24 = 4!. An exact integer, so this case is asserted with no ROUND wrapper at all and catches any accumulation of floating-point error in a series or Lanczos approximation.

GAUSS_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the probability of falling between the mean and 2 standard deviations
GAUSS_doc_example.notes: PUBLISHED EXAMPLE TABLE IS BROKEN, so the figure is taken from the page's prose and then derived. The GAUSS page's example table has a Formula column reading '=GAUSS(2) (with a leading apostrophe, i.e. the formula as literal text) and a Result column whose cell contains the string '=GAUSS(2)' rather than any number -- the table's own result cell was never evaluated. The only figure Microsoft actually publishes for this example is inside the Description column: "Probability that a member of a standard normal population will fall between the mean and 2 standard deviations from the mean (result is 0.47725)". Derived independently with mpmath at 50 digits from the definition the page gives -- GAUSS(z) = NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) - 0.5 = erf(z/sqrt(2))/2 -- giving 0.4772498680518207928, which rounds to exactly the published 0.47725.

GAUSS_zero_is_zero.description: At z = 0 the probability of falling between the mean and the mean is zero
GAUSS_zero_is_zero.notes: Derived from the identity the page itself states: "Because NORM.S.DIST(0,True) always returns 0.5, GAUSS(z) will always be 0.5 less than NORM.S.DIST(z,True)." At z = 0 that is 0.5 - 0.5 = 0 exactly. An exact value, so asserted with no ROUND wrapper.

GAUSS_matches_norm_s_dist_identity.description: The page's stated relationship to NORM.S.DIST, asserted as an exact difference
GAUSS_matches_norm_s_dist_identity.notes: Microsoft states: "Because NORM.S.DIST(0,True) always returns 0.5, GAUSS (z) will always be 0.5 less than NORM.S.DIST(z,True)." Written as a difference computed inside the engine under test, so it holds an engine to its OWN normal distribution rather than to a figure from outside -- an engine whose erf is slightly off passes only if both functions are off together, which is what the identity actually claims.

GAUSS_is_odd.description: GAUSS is an odd function, so GAUSS(-z) = -GAUSS(z)
GAUSS_is_odd.notes: Not published; derived from the definition. The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so the signed area from the mean out to -z is the negative of the area out to +z. mpmath at 50 digits: GAUSS(-2) = -0.4772498680518207928 exactly negates GAUSS(2). This is worth asserting because an implementation built on a one-sided series or table can easily return the ABSOLUTE probability 0.47725 for a negative z.

GAUSS_text_value.notes: Excel documents: "If z is not a valid data type, GAUSS returns the #VALUE! error value." (The page's companion clause, "If z is not a valid number, GAUSS returns the #NUM! error value", is not asserted anywhere in this corpus because the page never says which numbers are not valid ones -- the whole real line has a finite answer -- and this corpus does not invent an input to fit an undocumented guard.)

HYPGEOM.DIST_doc_example_cumulative.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cumulative hypergeometric distribution
HYPGEOM.DIST_doc_example_cumulative.notes: Microsoft publishes '=HYPGEOM.DIST(A2,A3,A4,A5,TRUE)' with the result 0.4654. Derived independently from the equation the page states -- P(X = x) = C(M,x)*C(N-M,n-x)/C(N,n) with x = sample_s, n = number_sample, M = population_s, N = number_pop -- evaluated in exact rational arithmetic from binomial coefficients rather than from any statistics library's hypergeometric routine: C(8,1)*C(12,3)/C(20,4) = 8*220/4845 = 1760/4845 = 0.36326109391124871001, and C(8,0)*C(12,4)/C(20,4) = 495/4845 = 0.10216718266253869969. The cumulative value is the sum of those two probability masses (x = 0 and x = 1), 2255/4845 = 0.4654282765737874097, which rounds to exactly the published 0.4654. Asserting the cumulative form alongside the mass form is the point of the modern name: HYPGEOM.DIST's whole reason for existing over HYPGEOMDIST is the cumulative argument. Set up from Microsoft's own worked-example table: A2 = 1 (number of successes in the sample), A3 = 4 (sample size), A4 = 8 (number of successes in the population) and A5 = 20 (population size), pasted at A1 as the page describes. Column F is untouched because this harness writes the formula under test into cell F1.

IMABS_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the modulus of 5+12i
IMABS_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMABS("5+12i")' with the result 13. Derived independently from the definition the page states, |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2): sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13 exactly. A Pythagorean triple was chosen by Microsoft precisely so the answer is an exact integer, so this is asserted with no ROUND wrapper -- any floating-point drift shows up immediately.

IMABS_second_triple.description: A second exact-integer modulus, from the 3-4-5 triple
IMABS_second_triple.notes: Not published on the IMABS page, but 3+4i is the complex number Microsoft's own IMAGINARY, IMARGUMENT, IMCONJUGATE and IMLN pages all use, so this ties the whole family to one number. sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 exactly.

IMABS_negative_components.description: Both components negative: a modulus is always non-negative
IMABS_negative_components.notes: Derived from |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), which squares away both signs: sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. Included because an implementation that parses the string by splitting on the sign characters, rather than by reading a signed real and a signed imaginary part, mis-handles a leading minus.

IMABS_j_suffix.description: The same number written with the documented j suffix instead of i
IMABS_j_suffix.notes: Microsoft documents every IM* function as accepting "a complex number in x + yi or x + yj text format", so the j suffix is not an alternative spelling this corpus invented -- it is half of the documented input grammar, and an engine that parses only the i form is incompatible on documented input. Same derivation as the doc example: sqrt(25 + 144) = 13.

IMABS_unit_imaginary.description: The bare imaginary unit, written with no coefficient and no real part
IMABS_unit_imaginary.notes: |i| = 1. This is the parsing edge case of the whole family: "i" carries neither a real part nor an explicit coefficient, and it is exactly the form Excel itself PRINTS for a result whose real part is 0 and whose imaginary coefficient is 1, so an engine that cannot read it back cannot round-trip its own output.

IMABS_plain_number.description: A plain real number, which is a complex number with zero imaginary part
IMABS_plain_number.notes: Microsoft's IMAGINARY page establishes that a bare number is a valid inumber by publishing '=IMAGINARY(4)' with the result 0. A real 4 therefore has modulus sqrt(16 + 0) = 4.

IMAGE_existence_probe.description: Existence probe only: the documented single-argument form, recorded without an asserted expected value
IMAGE_existence_probe.notes: NOT REPRODUCIBLE OFFLINE, and recorded as a probe rather than as a support claim -- the same treatment batch B gave COPILOT and the CUBE* family and batch C gave DETECTLANGUAGE. Microsoft's IMAGE page documents the function as inserting an image "from a source location" given "The URL path, using an 'https' protocol, of the image file", and its own error vocabulary is made of network and policy outcomes rather than computed values: #CONNECT! The successful return value is not a value at all in the spreadsheet sense -- it is an image rendered in the cell -- so there is nothing a .xlsx round trip could read back and compare, and no offline engine could produce it. IMAGINARY_doc_example.description: Microsoft's first worked example: the imaginary coefficient of 3+4i
IMAGINARY_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMAGINARY("3+4i")' with the result 4. Read directly off the documented x + yi form, where y is the imaginary coefficient.

IMAGINARY_doc_example_negative_j.description: Microsoft's second worked example: a j suffix, no explicit coefficient, negative sign
IMAGINARY_doc_example_negative_j.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMAGINARY("0-j")' with the result -1. Three separate parsing rules have to hold at once for this: the j suffix is accepted (Microsoft documents every IM* function as accepting "a complex number in x + yi or x + yj text format", so the j suffix is not an alternative spelling this corpus invented -- it is half of the documented input grammar, and an engine that parses only the i form is incompatible on documented input.), an absent coefficient means 1, and the sign attaches to that implied 1. This is the richest single parsing case Microsoft publishes anywhere in the IM* family.

IMAGINARY_doc_example_real_number.description: Microsoft's third worked example: a plain real number has imaginary coefficient 0
IMAGINARY_doc_example_real_number.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMAGINARY(4)' with the result 0 -- and it is the line that establishes, for the whole family, that a bare number is a legal complex argument.

IMAGINARY_unit_imaginary.description: The bare imaginary unit with no sign and no real part
IMAGINARY_unit_imaginary.notes: The positive counterpart of Microsoft's published "0-j" example: an absent coefficient means 1, so IMAGINARY("i") is +1. Asserted because "i" is the form Excel prints for the unit imaginary, so an engine that cannot read it cannot consume its own output.

IMARGUMENT_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the argument (theta) of 3+4i in radians
IMARGUMENT_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMARGUMENT("3+4i")' with the result 0.92729522. Derived independently with mpmath at 50 digits as atan2(4, 3) = 0.92729521800161223243, which rounds to exactly the published 0.92729522 at the 8 dp the page prints; asserted at 12 dp. Cross-check from a completely different direction: this same number is the imaginary part of Microsoft's own published IMLN("3+4i") result, 1.6094379124341+0.927295218001612i, since ln(z) = ln|z| + i*arg(z) -- two Microsoft pages independently agreeing on the same constant.

IMARGUMENT_eighth_turn.notes: Not published; derived from atan2(1, 1) = pi/4 = 0.78539816339744830962 (mpmath, 50 digits). Chosen because the answer is a recognizable closed form, so a wrong value is obviously wrong rather than merely different.

IMARGUMENT_negative_real_axis.description: The argument of -1 is pi, which is where a two-argument arctangent is required
IMARGUMENT_negative_real_axis.notes: Derived from atan2(0, -1) = pi = 3.1415926535897932385. This is the case that distinguishes a correct implementation from one built on the single-argument arctangent of y/x: that shortcut computes atan(0/-1) = atan(0) = 0 and loses the quadrant entirely, returning 0 instead of pi. Microsoft's page states the relationship as tan(theta) = y/x, which is exactly the ambiguous form, so the quadrant convention has to be inferred from the published example (3+4i, first quadrant) plus the standard principal-value range -- and this case is what makes that inference testable.

IMCONJUGATE_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the complex conjugate of 3+4i
IMCONJUGATE_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMCONJUGATE("3+4i")' with the result 3-4i, a string. Derived from the definition: the conjugate negates the imaginary part and leaves the real part alone. EXCEL'S COMPLEX-STRING FORMAT, which this corpus derives rather than assumes: a result is rendered as the real part, then the sign, then the imaginary coefficient followed by the suffix, with each part printed to at most 15 significant digits and trailing zeros stripped; a zero real part is omitted entirely, a zero imaginary part reduces the result to a bare real number, and an imaginary coefficient of exactly 1 or -1 prints as "i" / "-i" with no digit. That rule was not taken on faith -- it was written as a formatter in Python and validated against SEVEN independently published Microsoft strings in this batch alone (IMCOS, IMCOSH, IMCOT, IMCSC, IMCSCH, IMEXP and IMLN), which it reproduces byte for byte, before being used to predict any value this corpus asserts. String results are compared exactly, so a formatting-only difference (a trailing zero, "1i" for "i", a different digit count) fails the case and is recorded as its own divergence class, separate from a wrong numeric value.

IMCOS_logical_value.description: A logical argument, which the page rejects outright
IMCOS_logical_value.notes: Excel documents, on this page specifically: "If inumber is a logical value, IMCOS returns the #VALUE! error value." This is a deliberate refusal to coerce, and it is the sort of guard an engine drops: TRUE coerces to 1 in almost every other numeric context, so an implementation that simply converts its argument to a number computes cos(1) = 0.54030230586814 and returns a plausible answer where Excel raises an error. EXECUTED RESULT, and a SILENT WRONG ANSWER: all four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) return the string "0.54030230586814" -- that is cos(1), i.e. TRUE was coerced to 1 and fed to the function -- where the page documents #VALUE!. The same coercion happens on this batch's IMCOSH, IMCOT, IMCSC and IMCSCH when they are called under their unprefixed names (returning cosh(1), cot(1), csc(1) and csch(1) respectively), so it is one behaviour across the complex family rather than a slip in one function.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#VALUE!', got '0.54030230586814'

IMCOSH_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the hyperbolic cosine of 4+3i

That rule was not taken on faith -- it was written as a formatter in Python and validated against SEVEN independently published Microsoft strings in this batch alone (IMCOS, IMCOSH, IMCOT, IMCSC, IMCSCH, IMEXP and IMLN), which it reproduces byte for byte, before being used to predict any value this corpus asserts. String results are compared exactly, so a formatting-only difference (a trailing zero, "1i" for "i", a different digit count) fails the case and is recorded as its own divergence class, separate from a wrong numeric value. STORAGE-FORM GAP, and NOT a missing capability -- the distinction is the whole point of this case. IMCOSH is an Excel 2013 addition, so real Excel does not store it in a .xlsx under its plain name: Microsoft's XLSX-extensions future-function list (the reference this harness has used since batch A, mirrored in XlsxWriter's "Formulas added in Excel 2010 and later" table) gives the storage token as _xlfn.IMCOSH, alongside _xlfn.IMCOSH, _xlfn.IMCOT, _xlfn.IMCSC, _xlfn.IMCSCH, _xlfn.IMSEC, _xlfn.IMSECH, _xlfn.IMSINH and _xlfn.IMTAN. harness/xlfn_map.py therefore writes _xlfn.IMCOSH here, exactly as Excel would. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) return #NAME? for that token. A five-spelling probe pins down what this is: _xlfn.IMCOSH, COM.MICROSOFT.IMCOSH, ORG.OPENOFFICE.IMCOSH and _xlfn.ORG.OPENOFFICE.IMCOSH are all #NAME? on every build, while the UNPREFIXED IMCOSH(...) evaluates on every build and returns exactly the string asserted here, byte for byte. So LibreOffice implements IMCOSH correctly, and its OOXML import simply has no mapping for the _xlfn.IMCOSH token Excel writes -- meaning a workbook saved by Excel that uses IMCOSH arrives in LibreOffice as #NAME? even though LibreOffice could compute it. IMPOWER_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 2+3i raised to the power of 3
IMPOWER_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMPOWER("2+3i", 3)' with the result -46+9.00000000000001i, and its own Description column concedes the exact answer in parentheses: "(-46 + 9i)". Both are asserted correctly by the same derivation, and the gap between them is the point of this case. Exactly: (2+3i)^3 = 8 + 36i + 54i^2 + 27i^3 = 8 + 36i - 54 - 27i = -46 + 9i, an exact Gaussian integer. IMPRODUCT_doc_two_complex.description: Microsoft's first documented worked example: the product of two complex numbers
IMPRODUCT_doc_two_complex.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMPRODUCT("3+4i","5-3i")' with the result 27+11i. Derived independently from the identity the page renders as an image, (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i: ac-bd = 15 - (-12) = 27 and ad+bc = -9 + 20 = 11. Exact integer arithmetic -- no rounding is involved at any step, so this case tests the multiplication and the string format and nothing else. EXCEL'S COMPLEX-STRING FORMAT, which this corpus derives rather than assumes: a result is rendered as the real part, then the sign, then the imaginary coefficient followed by the suffix, with each part printed to at most 15 significant digits and trailing zeros stripped; a zero real part is omitted entirely, a zero imaginary part reduces the result to a bare real number, and an imaginary coefficient of exactly 1 or -1 prints as "i" / "-i" with no digit. That rule was written as a formatter in Python by batch D and validated against seven independently published Microsoft strings (IMCOS, IMCOSH, IMCOT, IMCSC, IMCSCH, IMEXP, IMLN); batch E re-ran that validation and then extended it, reproducing THIRTEEN MORE published Microsoft strings byte for byte (IMLOG10, IMLOG2, IMPOWER, both IMPRODUCT examples, IMSEC, IMSECH, IMSIN, IMSINH, IMSQRT, IMSUB, IMSUM, IMTAN) before predicting anything -- twenty published strings in all. ONE REFINEMENT BATCH E HAD TO MAKE: batch D fed the formatter the EXACT value computed at 40 digits, which happened to render identically to the IEEE double for all seven of its strings. That is not true here. A spreadsheet engine holds a double, not the exact value, and two of this batch's published strings only come out right if the derivation rounds to the nearest double BEFORE formatting: IMPOWER("2+3i",3) is exactly -46+9i in exact arithmetic but Microsoft publishes -46+9.00000000000001i, which is what exp(3*ln(2+3i)) gives in double precision; and IMSEC("4+3i") has an exact real part of -0.06529402785794704644..., whose 15-digit rounding ends ...47, while the correctly-rounded double -0.065294027857947051 rounds to ...471, which is what Microsoft publishes. So every value in this batch is derived exactly with mpmath at 40 digits, THEN rounded to the double an engine actually holds, THEN formatted. String results are compared exactly, so a formatting-only difference (a trailing zero, "1i" for "i", a different digit count) fails the case and is recorded as its own divergence class, separate from a wrong numeric value.

IMREAL_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the real coefficient of 6-9i
IMREAL_doc_example.notes: Microsoft publishes '=IMREAL("6-9i")' with the result 6. Exact and definitional: the real coefficient of x+yi is x. Note the result is a NUMBER, not one of the complex strings the rest of the IM* family returns -- IMREAL and IMAGINARY are the two extractors, and this corpus compares their results numerically rather than as text.

IMREAL_pure_imaginary_is_zero.description: A pure imaginary number, whose real coefficient is zero
IMREAL_pure_imaginary_is_zero.notes: Exact: 4i parses as 0+4i, so the real coefficient is 0. The mirror of the documented example, and the case that distinguishes "the real part is zero" from "there is no real part" -- the argument is written with no real term at all, exactly as the IM* format prints such numbers.

IMREAL_j_suffix.description: The x+yj form the page also documents
IMREAL_j_suffix.notes: The page's description says "in x + yi or x + yj text format", so the j suffix is documented. The real coefficient of 3+4j is 3 by the same definition.

IMSEC_doc_example.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the secant of 4+3i

STORAGE-FORM GAP, and NOT a missing capability -- the distinction is the whole point of this case. IMSEC is an Excel 2013 addition, so real Excel does not store it in a .xlsx under its plain name: Microsoft's XLSX-extensions future-function list (the reference this harness has used since batch A, mirrored in XlsxWriter's "Formulas added in Excel 2010 and later" table) gives the storage token as _xlfn.IMSEC, alongside _xlfn.IMCOSH, _xlfn.IMCOT, _xlfn.IMCSC, _xlfn.IMCSCH, _xlfn.IMSEC, _xlfn.IMSECH, _xlfn.IMSINH and _xlfn.IMTAN. harness/xlfn_map.py therefore writes _xlfn.IMSEC here, exactly as Excel would. EXECUTED RESULT: all four LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) return #NAME? for that token. A five-spelling probe pins down what this is: _xlfn.IMSEC, COM.MICROSOFT.IMSEC, ORG.OPENOFFICE.IMSEC and _xlfn.ORG.OPENOFFICE.IMSEC are all #NAME? on every build, while the UNPREFIXED IMSEC(...) evaluates on every build and returns exactly the string asserted here, byte for byte. So LibreOffice implements IMSEC, and its OOXML import simply has no mapping for the _xlfn.IMSEC token Excel writes -- meaning a workbook saved by Excel that uses IMSEC arrives in LibreOffice as #NAME? even though LibreOffice could compute it. This is the exact mirror image of batch B's COT/COTH/CSC/CSCH finding, where the _xlfn. token was the ONLY spelling LibreOffice accepted, and it is the same class batch D recorded for IMCOSH, IMCOT, IMCSC and IMCSCH. It is recorded as its own divergence class rather than as an ordinary unsupported-function result. CROSS-VERSION DRIFT FOUND HERE, in the last digit. Under the unprefixed name the four builds do NOT agree: 24.2.0.3 and 24.8.7.2 return -0.0652940278579471-0.0752249603027732i, which is Microsoft's published string byte for byte, while 25.2.0.3 and 25.8.7.3 return -0.065294027857947-0.0752249603027732i -- one significant digit shorter. Neither is a wrong value: the exact real part is -0.06529402785794704644515821, the correctly-rounded double is -0.065294027857947051 (whose 15-digit rendering ends ...471, matching Excel and the older builds) and the newer builds hold the adjacent double -0.065294027857947037 (whose 15-digit rendering ends ...47). The two doubles differ by one unit in the last place, about 1.4e-17, and straddle a 15-digit rounding boundary, which is the only reason the STRINGS differ at all. Recorded as a precision/formatting difference, not as a value error -- but it is a real regression in byte-for-byte agreement with Excel, and because IM* results are strings, an exact-match comparison in a spreadsheet would flag it.; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '-0.0652940278579471-0.0752249603027732i', got '#NAME?'

INFO returns facts about the machine the workbook is open on, so no fixed value can be asserted for most type_text codes without pinning the assertion to this VM instead of to the function.
